item.title: Cherry Hallway Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — fully dimensioned and detailed, but not yet cut. A narrow wall console for an entry/hallway: drop keys and mail on top, baskets or shoes on the lower shelf. Solid cherry, hand-tool build (stock ripped and thickness-planed by machine; all joinery cut by hand).

  • Overall size: 42" W × 14" D × 34" H
  • Top overhang: 1" all around the leg frame
  • Lower shelf: ~10" off the floor, resting on the lower rails
  • Joinery: mortise-and-tenon frame, drawbored; floating solid top

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Leg layout (mortise heights and drawbore pin positions)

The drawing shows the front-left leg. The back-right leg is the same part turned end for end, and the front-right and back-left legs are its mirror image. Mortise length depends on the tenon width (and any haunch at the top of the leg), which this plan doesn’t fix, so the shaded strips mark only where each mortise sits across the face and which height band it falls in.

Variant: want somewhere to sit and put shoes on? See Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench — the same console with an open lower half and a blanket-chest seat that slides underneath.

Why these proportions

The shallow 14" depth is the point of a hallway piece — it hugs the wall and stays out of the traffic path. 34" tall sits at about waist height, comfortable for setting things down (anywhere 30–34" works; taller reads more console-like). 42" long gives presence without dominating a corridor. Legs are 1½" square — slender but honest for this span; go to 1¾" if you want it chunkier. The lower shelf earns its keep both as storage and as a structural tie that stiffens the whole frame.

Materials

Species: solid cherry, clear finish. Cherry darkens dramatically with light over the first few months (pale pink → deep reddish-brown) — plan around that (see notes).

Stock Used for Rough qty (approx)
8/4 (2" rough) Legs only 5–6 bd ft
4/4 (1" rough) Top, aprons, lower rails, shelf 18–20 bd ft

Only the legs need stock heavier than 4/4. A finished 1½"-square leg cannot come out of 4/4 — rough 4/4 only nets ~¾" of flat, clean stock after jointing and planing out cup/twist. Buy 8/4 and keep the legs seamless. (6/4 is too close to 1½" finished to survive jointing unless you drop the legs to ~1⅜".)

Lamination alternative: two face-glued pieces of 4/4 make a ~1½" blank, but on a 1½"-square leg the glue line lands on two visible faces and will age to a slightly different shade. On a clear-finished cherry piece, 8/4 is worth it. If you do laminate, orient the seam to a back corner.

The 4/4 estimate leaves margin for grain-matching the top and shelf glue-ups and for working around cherry’s gum streaks and sapwood.

Cut list

Dimensions are thickness × width × length. Cut to the length in the table — the tenon lengths are already baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L (cut to this) Tenons / notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½" × 1½" × 33¼" Mortised on two adjacent faces
Long aprons (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Long lower rails (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short lower rails (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Top 1 4/4 ¾" × 14" × 42" No joinery; floats on frame
Lower shelf 1 4/4 ¾" × 12" × 40" Notch corners 1½" × 1½"; rests on rails

Key reference dimensions

  • Shoulder-to-shoulder (what actually keeps the frame square):
    • Long aprons & long rails: 37"
    • Short aprons & short rails: 9"
  • The extra 2" on each part = two 1" tenons living inside the legs. Set your shoulder gauge to 37" / 9" and the tenon length falls out on its own.
  • Mortises: ~5/16" wide × ~1" deep. Two tenons meet inside each leg corner — miter their tips at 45° so they don’t collide.

Build sequence

  1. Mill 4/4 down to a true ¾" in stages, resting between passes — cherry moves as internal tension releases. Leave leg blanks a hair oversized off the planer and take the last shaving by hand.
  2. Lay out and cut all mortises and tenons. Fit each tenon to its mortise before any glue-up.
  3. Glue up two end units: each = a pair of legs + short apron + short lower rail.
  4. Connect the two ends with the long aprons and long rails.
  5. Dry-clamp the whole frame and confirm the 37" and 9" shoulder distances land square before committing.
  6. Drawbore the tenons — pins pull the joints tight without clamping across the 42" span. See Drawboring below for sizes and the step-by-step.
  7. Drop the shelf onto the four lower rails.
  8. Attach the top with figure-8 fasteners or wooden buttons so the solid top can float (expand/contract seasonally). Do not glue the top down.

Drawboring

Drawboring means the pin hole in the leg and the pin hole in the tenon are deliberately about 1/32″ out of line. A tapered pin driven through both pulls the tenon deeper into the mortise and closes the shoulder, then locks the joint mechanically. On a 42″ frame that replaces a long clamp, and the joint stays tight even if the glue ever lets go.

The blue hole is drilled in the leg; the red hole is drilled in the tenon, centered 1/32″ nearer the shoulder. The section looks down through a front leg at one of the front-apron pins. It also shows the side-apron tenon meeting the front-apron tenon at their mitred tips. The drawing is true to scale.

Sizes for this table

Item Value Why
Pin diameter 1/8″ The tenon is only 5/16″ thick; a 1/4″ pin would leave ~1/32″ of wood each side
Offset 1/32″ toward the shoulder Hardwood pins this small tolerate up to ~3/64″; more can crush or split the tenon
Pin position ½″ in from the leg face Mid-tenon on a 1″ tenon, clear of the end grain and of the mitered tip of the neighboring tenon
Pins per tenon 2 on the 3½″ aprons (about 1″ from each edge); 1–2 on the 2½″ rails Spreads the pull across the width of the tenon
Hole depth in leg Through the near wall, across the mortise, ¼″ into the far wall Blind, so no pin end shows on the far side

Stagger the pins at each leg corner. Two tenons meet inside the leg, and their pins are drilled from the two adjacent outer faces. If the long-apron pin and the short-apron pin sit at the same height they cross inside the leg. Put the long-apron pins at about ¾″ and 2¾″ below the top edge, and the short-apron pin at about 1¾″ (mid-height).

Steps

  1. Cut and fit every mortise and tenon dry. It should seat by hand or with light taps, not with force.
  2. Drill the leg. Use a sharp brad-point bit and a backing block. Start on the leg’s outer face (so the pin dots show on the faces that are meant to be seen) and drill square through the near wall, across the mortise, and ¼″ into the far wall.
  3. Mark the tenon. Seat the tenon fully, put the bit back into the leg hole and tap it so the point dimples the tenon cheek.
  4. Offset and drill the tenon. Pull the tenon, move the mark 1/32″ toward the shoulder, and drill at that new mark. A drill press with a fence keeps it square to the cheek; clamp scrap behind to prevent blowout.
  5. Make the pins. Straight-grain cherry or 1/8″ hardwood dowel, with a 3/8″ taper at the tip so it finds the offset hole.
  6. Glue-up. Glue on the tenon cheeks and shoulders, none on the pins. Seat the joint, then drive the pin until it stops; you should feel the shoulder draw in.
  7. When the glue has set, saw the pins flush and scrape them clean.

For this build

  • Do the end units first (short, easy), then assemble the long aprons and rails into both ends together. Use hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you are not racing the clock over 42″.
  • Drive the pins one corner at a time. A single pipe clamp is only for starting the joints, not for holding them.
  • Test on scrap first: make one joint in cherry with the same 5/16″ tenon and 1/8″ pin. A good result is a closed shoulder with no cracks around the pin; if the tenon splits, reduce the offset.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut the apron joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The plan’s 5/16″ mortise is 7.9 mm, so an 8 mm Domino matches it, and a 40 mm Domino sits 20 mm (¾″) deep in each part.

The one rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside a 1½″ leg. The hand-cut plan avoids that by mitering the tenon tips. Loose tenons can’t be mitered, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them.

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Long aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 24 mm (≈ 15/16″) below the apron’s top edge 37″ (39″)
Short aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 66 mm (≈ 2⅝″) below the apron’s top edge 9″ (11″)
Lower rails (×4) Keep the hand-cut mitered tenons 39″ and 11″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (37″ and 9″); there is no tenon allowance to add.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg faces and centre each 8 mm mortise on the apron’s ¾″ thickness.
  • The 2½″ lower rails are too short to stagger two 40 mm Dominoes at the same corner, so they stay hand-cut. Their mortises sit well below the apron Dominoes, so nothing collides.
  • One 8×40 Domino has noticeably less glue area than the full-width tenon it replaces. That is fine for a hallway console; the lower rails and shelf stiffen the frame.
  • Drawboring does not carry over to the Domino joints (a 1/8″ pin through an 8 mm Domino is marginal). Clamp the aprons instead, with hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you can square a 42″ frame before it sets.

Hand-tool & cherry notes

  • Tear-out: cherry planes beautifully but tears where grain reverses (near figure or the pith). Keep the smoother sharp and finely set, read grain direction before each pass, and keep a card scraper handy for the top glue-up and any tricky patches.
  • Color / clamps: don’t leave clamps, tape, or stickers on exposed surfaces during glue-up or curing — cherry tans unevenly and you’ll get pale patches that never catch up.
  • Squeeze-out: scrape off all glue squeeze-out before finishing. Finish over dried glue blocks the darkening and leaves permanent ghost lines.

Adjustments to consider

  • Stretch to 48" long, or drop height to 30".
  • Add a drawer in the front apron (would change the front apron to a rail + drawer pocket).
  • Bump legs to 1¾" square for a heavier look (still cut from 8/4).

item.title: Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed two-piece build: the Cherry Hallway Console reworked so its lower half is open, plus a separate blanket chest that doubles as a seat and slides underneath. Sit on the lid to put shoes on; push the chest in and the hallway looks like a plain console. Solid cherry, drawbored mortise-and-tenon frame, dovetailed chest.

Everything here is my own design, so there are no maker dimensions to match. Every number is a design choice or derived from one, and the fit checks below show how the two pieces close.

What changes from the original console

Original This version Why
Overall 42″ × 14″ × 34″ 42″ × 15″ × 35″ 1″ deeper so the seat is 13″ deep (shoe-tying depth); 1″ taller so the lid can open fully under the apron
Lower shelf Yes, ≈ 10″ off floor Removed The chest lives there
Front lower rail Yes Removed The chest slides in through the front
Back lower rail Yes Kept — now the chest’s stop
Side lower rails Yes Kept The chest passes between them
Leg frame 40″ × 12″ 40″ × 13″

How the two pieces fit

Check Working Result
Opening between front legs 40 − 2 × 1½ 37″
Chest width 37 − 2 × ½ clearance 36″
Side rails, inner faces 40 − 2 × ¾ 38½″ apart — chest never touches them
Clear height under the apron 35 − ¾ top − 3½ apron 30¾″
Seat (lid top) height design choice 17″ — a normal bench height
Space above the lid 30¾ − 17 13¾″
Lid depth (hinged at the back) 13″
Lid front edge, open to vertical 17 + 13 30″, so ¾″ below the apron
Back stop 15 − 1 − ¾ (back rail) chest back at 13¼″ from the front edge
Chest front 13¼ − 13 ¼″ behind the top’s front edge, ¾″ proud of the legs

The lid opens all the way with the chest pushed fully under — the lid’s front edge swings up an arc of radius 13″ and clears the apron by ¾″. A deeper chest or a taller seat would break that, so the 17″ × 13″ pair is the limit for this console. For comfortable access to blankets, slide the chest out a few inches first.

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px (the two chest drawings at 1″ = 16 px). Click to open full size.

Front elevation, chest pushed in

Side elevation, lid open to vertical

Plan view, top removed

Chest end section

Chest front elevation

Console

Joinery and finishing are the same as the original plan: mortise-and-tenon, 1″ tenons, drawbored, floating top on buttons or figure-8s. See its Drawboring section for pin sizes and steps.

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length. Tenon lengths are baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½″ × 1½″ × 34¼″
Long aprons (front, back) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 39″ 37″ shoulder to shoulder
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 12″ 10″ shoulder to shoulder
Side lower rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 12″ Top edge ≈ 9¼″ off the floor, flush to the leg outer face
Back lower rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 39″ The chest’s stop; glue a ¼″ felt strip on its inner face
Top 1 4/4 ¾″ × 15″ × 42″ Floats; 1″ overhang all round

Stiffness without a front lower rail

With the front rail gone, the base is braced on three sides (two side rails and the back rail) and the top is a rigid box of four 3½″ aprons. That is enough for a hallway piece, but it relies on the joints: drawbore the apron joints, and dry-assemble to check there is no racking along the 42″ length before you glue. If the front legs still flex, add a hidden gusset block at each front leg-to-apron corner.

Chest bench

Cut list

Cherry for everything visible. T × W × L.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Lid 1 5/4 1″ × 13″ × 36″ Glue up from two boards; cleat underneath (below)
Case front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 36″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Case ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 13″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Bottom 1 ½″ ½″ × 11⅞″ × 35″ Cherry or ply; floats in the grooves, grain along the length if solid
Plinth front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 35¼″ Mitered corners, inset ⅜″ all round
Plinth ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 12¼″ Mitered corners
Lid cleats 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1¼″ × 11¼″ Underside, 2″ in from each end; slotted screw holes so the lid can move

Height is 1″ lid + 13¾″ case + 2¼″ plinth = 17″. The interior is about 34½″ × 11½″ × 13″ (the ½″ bottom sits in grooves ¼″ up from the case’s bottom edge).

Hardware

  • Hinge: one 36″ continuous (piano) hinge, 1½″ open, mortised into the back edge of the lid and case.
  • Lid support: two soft-close lid stays rated for the lid’s weight (≈ 10 lb), so it can’t slam on fingers.
  • Glides: four PTFE or felt glide pads under the plinth so the chest slides on a hard floor.
  • Edges: ease the lid edges ⅛″–¼″; they are where you sit.

Build sequence

  1. Mill case, lid and plinth stock and let it settle between passes.
  2. Cut and fit the through dovetails on the case. Plow the ¼″ bottom grooves before assembly.
  3. Glue up the case with the bottom dry (unglued) in its grooves.
  4. Make the plinth, miter the corners, and glue it to the case bottom edge — long grain to long grain, so glue is fine.
  5. Glue up the lid, add the cleats, and mortise the hinge into lid and case.
  6. Hang the lid and fit the stays. Check the lid opens to vertical with the chest in place under the console.
  7. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax; add glides last.

Open questions

  • Seat depth. 13″ is comfortable for shoes but shallow for general sitting. Going deeper means a deeper, taller console so the lid still clears; the arc check above is the thing to redo.
  • Console leg section. 1½″ legs were fine for the original shelf version; with the front rail gone you may prefer 1¾″.
  • Floor type. Glides assume a hard floor; for carpet use rigid plastic skids instead.

item.title: Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Woods Studios / Vermont Furniture Designs Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console Table (product page, archive), with the proportions held to the maker’s published numbers. A long, low console: a wide, thin top that overhangs the leg frame by a lot at the ends, two shallow drawers hung right under the top, and a narrow lower shelf carried on chunky side rails.

Provenance of the numbers. Dimensions marked (stated) come straight from the maker’s Dimensions and Construction Details panels. Dimensions marked (derived) are worked out from the stated ones so everything closes. Dimensions marked (est.) are measured off the maker’s front and three-quarter photos — good to roughly ±¼″ — and are the ones to sanity-check against the real piece, or against your own taste, before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value
Overall 60″ W × 16″ D × 29″ H (stated)
Top overhang, ends 8″ (stated)
Top overhang, front/back 1″ (stated)
Drawer front (exterior) 19.75″ W × 3.5″ H (stated)
Drawer interior 18″ W × 7.5″ D × 2″ H (stated)
Bottom shelf 41.5″ W × 9.75″ D (stated)
Species Cherry, maple or walnut (stated)
Drawers Dovetailed; beech sides, back and bottom; metal slides; walnut pulls (stated)
Finish Cherry/walnut: hand-rubbed linseed oil + wax. Maple: tung oil + wax (stated)

Drawings (true scale)

All five are generated from the dimensions on this page and drawn true to scale. The elevations and plan are at 1″ = 12 px, so they can be measured against each other; the drawer-bay detail and leg layout are drawn larger (scale on each). Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Drawer bay and drawer box

Leg layout

The ratios

Everything hangs off the 60″ overall width and the 8″ / 1″ overhangs. The frame is whatever is left:

Derived Working Result
Leg frame, width 60 − 2 × 8 44″ (derived)
Leg frame, depth 16 − 2 × 1 14″ (derived)
Frame opening between front legs 44 − 2 × 1¾ 40½″ (derived)
Two drawer fronts + divider + reveals 2 × 19.75 + ¾ + 4 × 1/16 40½″ (derived — fills the opening exactly)
Shelf width 44 − 2 × 1¼ (side-rail thickness) 41½″ (derived — matches stated shelf width)
Shoulder-to-shoulder, front↔back 14 − 2 × 1¾ 10½″ (derived; shelf is 9¾″, leaving ¾″)

That the two independent checks (drawers fill 40½″; shelf lands on 41½″ with 1¼″ rails) both close is the evidence that the 1¾″ legs and 1¼″-thick side rails are right.

Proportion Value
Width : height 60 : 29 ≈ 2.07 : 1
Width : depth 60 : 16 = 3.75 : 1
Frame width ÷ overall width 44 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.733 (each end overhang = 13.3 %)
Drawer front width ÷ overall width 19.75 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.33
Drawer front height ÷ overall height 3.5 ÷ 29 ≈ 0.12
Leg width ÷ overall height 1¾ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.06
Shelf top height ÷ overall height ≈ 10½ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.36 (est.)

To resize: multiply every dimension by one factor k (so 48″ long → k = 0.8) and the proportions hold. Round leg and rail sections to stock, but do not change the 8″-end / 1″-front overhang ratio independently of the width — the long ends are the look.

Dimensions that are estimates

Item Value Basis
Top thickness ¾″ (est.) ≈ 14 px against a 3.5″ drawer front at ≈ 66 px in the front photo. Could be 1″; ¾″ keeps the 8″ cantilever light
Leg section 1¾″ square (est.) ≈ 1.85″ measured, and 1¾″ is what makes both closures above work
Shelf top above floor ≈ 10½″ (est.) Front photo, scaled against the 29″ height
Lower drawer rail ¾″ thick × 1″ tall (est.) Thin strip under the drawers in the front photo
Center divider ¾″ wide (est.) Narrow stile between the drawers
Side aprons 4½″ tall (est.) Solid panel under the top at the ends in the three-quarter photo
Pull 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ (est.), walnut ≈ 8″ long against the 19.75″ drawer front; stand-off finger pull

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length — 1″ tenons are baked into rail and apron lengths. Species: cherry (or maple/walnut) for the case; beech (or maple) for drawer boxes.

Case

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 1¾″ × 1¾″ × 28¼″ 8/4 stock. Height = 29 − ¾ top
Lower front rail 1 ¾″ × 1″ × 42½″ Under the drawers; 40½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Back apron 1 ¾″ × 4½″ × 42½″ 1″ tenons
Side aprons 2 ¾″ × 4½″ × 12½″ 10½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Center divider 1 ¾″ × ¾″ × 3⅝″ Underside of top to lower front rail; pinned to the front of the center runner
Center runner 1 ¾″ × 3″ × 12½″ Lower front rail to back apron, centered; slides mount on both faces. Housed in both
Slide spacers 2 1″ × 3″ × 9″ Screwed to the inside of the side aprons so the slide face sits at the drawer-box edge
Shelf side rails 2 1¼″ × 2½″ × 12½″ Flush to leg outer faces; 10½″ between shoulders; top ≈ 11″ off floor
Shelf cleats 2 ¾″ × ¾″ × 9¾″ Glue/screw to rail inner faces to carry the shelf
Shelf 1 ¾″ × 9¾″ × 41½″ Sits between the side rails, centered front-to-back (⅜″ setback each side)
Top 1 ¾″ × 16″ × 60″ Floats; buttons or figure-8s, never glued

As listed, the spacers and runner put the slide faces 19⅞″ apart in each bay, which leaves 7/16″ per side beside the 19″ drawer box — 1/16″ per side less than the ½″ most side-mount slides need (see Open questions). Adjust them to the clearance of the slides you buy.

Drawers (×2, identical)

Part Qty each T × W × L Notes
Front 1 ¾″ × 3½″ × 19¾″ Cherry, grain-matched to the case; 1/16″ reveals all round
Sides 2 ½″ × 2½″ × 8½″ Beech; dovetailed to front and back
Back 1 ½″ × 2½″ × 18″ (between sides) Beech
Bottom 1 ¼″ × as fitted Beech; in a groove, floating
Pull 1 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ Walnut; two screws from the inside

The stated 18″ × 7½″ × 2″ interior sets the drawer box: 18″ clear between ½″ sides gives a box 19″ wide overall, which leaves 7/16″ per side in the 19⅞″ bay — not quite the ½″ per side that standard slides need (see Open questions). The 7½″ box depth sits in a 14″ frame, so there is room behind the drawers — decide whether to close it with a back panel (the maker uses plywood backs on case pieces) or leave it open.

Build sequence

  1. Mill legs from 8/4 and everything else to size; let stock sit between passes — cherry moves.
  2. Cut mortises and tenons (5/16″–⅜″ mortises, 1″ deep). Miter tenon tips where two meet inside a leg.
  3. Dry-fit the two end frames: leg pair + side apron + shelf side rail. Confirm the 10½″ shoulder distance and that the rail sits flush to the leg outer face.
  4. Glue up the ends, then join them with the front and back aprons and the lower front rail. Dry-clamp first and check the 40½″ opening and the 44″ × 14″ frame for square. Drawbore if you like — optional here, since the top and drawers add little racking load.
  5. Fit the center runner and divider and check the two drawer openings are equal (≈ 19⅞″ each with 1/16″ reveals).
  6. Screw on the slide spacers, add the shelf cleats and drop in the shelf. The shelf carries load, so keep the cleats glued and screwed.
  7. Build and dovetail the drawers, fit the slides, then trim the fronts to a 1/16″ reveal.
  8. Make the walnut pulls and fit them.
  9. Finish: hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax for cherry and walnut (tung oil and wax for maple), matching the maker. Scrape off all squeeze-out first.
  10. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Center it: 8″ at each end, 1″ front and back.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut most of the joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The 5/16″ mortise in this plan matches an 8 mm Domino; a 40 mm Domino goes 20 mm (¾″) into each part, a 50 mm Domino 25 mm (1″).

Rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them. (The hand-cut plan avoids this by mitering tenon tips, which a loose tenon can’t do.)

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Back apron (¾″ × 4½″) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 25 mm below the apron’s top edge 40½″ (42½″)
Side aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 70 mm below the apron’s top edge 10½″ (12½″)
Lower front rail (¾″ × 1″) 1 × 4×20 per end, centred on the rail 40½″ (42½″)
Shelf side rails (×2, 1¼″ × 2½″) 1 × 8×50 per end, centred 10½″ (12½″)
Center runner Keep it housed in the lower front rail and back apron 12½″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (40½″ and 10½″).
  • At the back legs the back apron (upper) and side apron (lower) are staggered. At the front legs the side apron (lower-middle of its 4½″) stays clear of the lower front rail’s 4×20.
  • The 1″ lower front rail is the weak spot — a 4×20 is the largest Domino that fits. It is lightly loaded and the center runner and divider support it, but if you want more, use a shop-made stub tenon.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg outer faces and centre each mortise on the part’s thickness.

Open questions

  • Top thickness — ¾″ is estimated; if the real piece reads chunkier, 1″ is the likely answer. Re-check drawer front height (3.5″) against it.
  • Shelf height — about 10½″ to the shelf top is estimated from photos.
  • Frame joinery — the maker’s page does not say how the legs and rails are joined, so mortise-and-tenon here is my choice, to match the other console plan on this site.
  • Space behind the drawers — see the note above.
  • Slide clearance — the stated 18″ interior with ½″ sides makes a 19″ box, but each bay is 19⅞″ between slide faces: 7/16″ per side, where ½″ slides need ½″. To fit them, either plane the drawer sides to 7/16″ (box 18⅞″, keeps the stated interior), take 1/16″ off each spacer and make the runner ⅝″ (bays 20″), or keep ½″ sides on a 17⅞″ interior.

item.title: Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Furniture Designs Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (product page, archive), with the proportions taken from the maker’s photos and drawing. Three equal drawers stacked under a top that flares out past the case at the ends, four straight legs, an arched apron across the front, and frame-and-panel sides.

Provenance of the numbers. The maker publishes only the overall size and the construction notes. (stated) = from the maker’s page. (derived) = worked out from other numbers here so everything closes. (est.) = measured off the maker’s front photo, dimensioned drawing and three-quarter photo — good to about ±¼″ at best. The front/back overhang in particular is borrowed from a sibling model (the Heartwood Shaker End Table), because it cannot be read from a front view. Check the (est.) items before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value

item.title: Jeweler's Traveling Tool Chest (Proposed)
item.description:
A tool chest for a jeweler who solders rings and pendants and teaches lapidary workshops (domed cabochons and flat/faceted stones). It has to do two jobs: sit on a bench as a daily soldering kit, and travel to a workshop with a lapidary teaching kit. Two classic chest styles fit; this page compares them, then lays out a proposed build modeled on Mike Pekovich’s traveling tool chest, resized and re-organized for jewelry and lapidary tools.

Provenance of the numbers. Pekovich’s chest is a course product, and its page publishes no dimensions, species or drawer count, so this is a design inspired by it, not a copy. (stated) = from the course page. (derived) = worked out from the sizes I chose so everything closes. (est.) = typical sizes of tools and supplies, which vary by brand: put your own tools on the bench and check them before cutting.

The finished chest (concept rendering)

Nothing here is built yet, so this is a drawing from the plan sizes, not a photograph.

Two styles to choose from

Pekovich traveling chest Dutch tool chest
Shape Rectangular case, flat frame-and-panel lid, drawers under an open well Sloped lid, two tiers, fall front (see below)
Made to Be carried: side handles, lock, modest size Hold a full set of woodworking hand tools
Strength Tidy small tools: lift-out tray, two drawers, lockable Big tools: planes, saws, chisels, in a light pine box
Weak point here A well too shallow for long tools Jeweler’s tools are small and need separating; a big open well does not give you that

Pick: the Pekovich style. A jeweler’s kit is hundreds of small, fragile or expensive pieces (stones, laps, burs, solder). They want dividers, a lock, and a carry size, and not a big open well. The standard Dutch chest, described next, is the better answer for planes and saws.

The standard Dutch tool chest

For comparison, this is the chest the Dutch style is known for: a woodworker’s tool chest, not a jeweler’s. I read two pages for it, so what follows is what they say and little more. Christopher Schwarz’s book Dutch Tool Chests is the place for dimensions and joinery; I could not open that page.

Item What the sources say
Lid “Perhaps the chest’s most distinctive characteristic is its sloped lid” (stated, Fine Woodworking). A search summary of a Schwarz video gives about 30°; I did not confirm it
Tiers A top tier for chisels, saws, planes and layout tools, and a bottom sized for molding and joinery planes and tool rolls (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Fall front Has battens; they work best when set no more than ⅛″ inside the case sides (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Joinery Dovetails at the bottom only, plus dadoes, rabbets and cut nails (stated, Fine Woodworking); screws are not required, and cut nails or wooden pegs work (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Wood Pine “or another lightweight wood”; “the cheapest, lightest wood that is available” (stated)
Size One build’s interior depth is 11¼″, the width of a 1×12 (stated, Fine Woodworking). Overall sizes are not stated in what I could read; the “big” chest is said to hold as many tools as a full-size English floor chest (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Hardware and finish Strap hinges and lifts; commonly painted, historically often blue (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Not found Overall dimensions, the side profile, dado heights, and any sliding or saw till

What it means for a jeweler’s chest. The Dutch chest suits a woodworker’s long, heavy tools in a light box that is simple to build. A jeweler’s kit is small and needs separating, which is why this page builds the Pekovich style. The one idea worth borrowing is the two tiers: small tools on top, heavier ones below. The proposed chest already does this with its tray and drawers.

What Pekovich’s course covers (stated)

From the course page (archive), titled Build a Traveling Tool Chest with Mike Pekovich:

Item Value

Shelf Through-tenons, laid out together with the mortises (stated)
Case assembly Glued up, tenons wedged, then drilled and pinned (stated)
Case front Mortised for a lid lock (stated)
Lid Frame-and-panel, with bridle joints at the corners (stated)
Drawers Pinned rabbet drawers (stated)
Storage Lift-out mitered trays, slotted blocks for saws, other tool-holding features (stated)
Level / length Intermediate; over 10 hours of instruction; downloadable plans (stated)
Not stated Overall size, species, drawer count, hinge type, handles

If you build from this page, buy the course for the joinery: this page does not teach it.

What the chest has to do

  • Hold two kits that are never used at the same time. Soldering (daily, bench) and lapidary (workshop days) go in separate drawers, so you can lift out one kit.
  • Stay light enough to carry. The case alone is about 22 lb in cherry (derived: ½″ case parts, ¾″ shelf and bottom, cherry at about 35 lb/ft³). Tools add roughly 15–20 lb (est.). Plan on two bail handles and, at about 40 lb loaded, a second person for stairs.
  • Keep the abrasives apart. In cabbing, a single grain of a coarse grit on a fine pad leaves scratches that cost a whole polishing step. Each grit gets its own sealed jar, and laps stay in their own sleeves.
  • Keep acid and water out. Pickle (Sparex or citric) and wet lapidary slurry corrode steel tools and stain wood. The chest holds dry, clean tools only; carry wet items in a separate tub.
  • Protect metal and stones. Many woods give off organic acids, and oak is the usual one to avoid near steel and silver. Use cherry or maple, finish the inside with dewaxed shellac, and wax it. Keep loose stones in lidded boxes or gem papers, not in open tray compartments.
  • Be lockable. A half-mortise lid lock (the course installs one) deters casual theft but does not stop a determined one. A chest with stones and precious metal also needs insurance, which a lock does not replace.

Build order

  1. Mock up and check the tools. Lay your actual tools on the tray and drawer footprints. Move dividers before cutting any wood. Most fixes here cost nothing.
  2. Mill the stock and cut the sides, well front, back, bottom and shelf to length.
  3. Cut the joints: dovetails for the well front and back, grooves for the bottom, rabbet for the back, mortises for the shelf’s through-tenons.
  4. Dry-fit, then glue the case. Wedge and pin the shelf tenons.
  5. Make the lid: bridle-jointed frame, floating panel, then hang it with two butt hinges and fit the stay and the lock.
  6. Fit the drawer rail, make the drawers, then plane the fronts to ¹⁄₁₆″ reveals.
  7. Make the tray and cleats, and cut the dividers last so they fit the finished drawers.
  8. Finish: dewaxed shellac inside, shellac and wax outside. Let it cure fully before you load the tools.
  9. Handles and pulls.

Open questions

  • What the workshops supply. This plan assumes the venue provides the grinders, trim saw and faceting machine, so the chest carries only hand tools and consumables. If you bring a faceting head or a small cab machine, it needs its own case.
  • The meaning of “flat/faceted ground.” I read it as flat-lapped and faceted stones next to domed cabochons. If it means something else, the laps and dops section changes.
  • Lap size. The laps drawer assumes 6″ discs. 8″ laps do not fit a 9⅝″ drawer with their sleeves, so check yours.
  • Weight. About 22 lb empty is heavy for a chest that will go up stairs. Basswood or poplar drawers, or ⅜″ case parts, save about 4 lb; I kept ½″ for the dovetails and handles.
  • Hinge, lock and handle choices. The course page does not name them; the ones above are my choice.

item.title: Mitered Picture Frame, 1¼″ × ⅞″ Profile (Proposed)
item.description:
A plain, square-profile mitered picture frame made from stock that is 1¼″ wide and ⅞″ tall, rabbeted on the back to hold glass, a picture and a backing board. The worked example is a picture 11½″ tall × 15⅝″ wide; a formula and a size table at the bottom give the numbers for any other picture.

Provenance of the numbers. (stated) = given by you: the stock profile and the picture size. (chosen) = a design decision I made because the profile alone doesn’t settle it (rabbet size, glass clearance). (derived) = worked out from those so everything closes. Change a (chosen) value and the (derived) ones move with it. The Alternate rabbet section shows how.

What is stated, what is chosen

Item Value
Stock profile 1¼″ wide × ⅞″ tall, square edges (stated)
Picture / glass 11½″ tall × 15⅝″ wide (stated); landscape
Rabbet ⅜″ wide × ½″ deep, cut on the back inside edge (chosen)
Glass-to-rabbet clearance 1/16″ each side (chosen)
Joint Four 45° miters

Why that rabbet: ½″ deep holds ⅛″ glass + the print (≤ 1/16″) + a ⅛″ backing board ≈ 5/16″ and still leaves ≈ 3/16″ for the retaining points. That leaves a ⅜″-thick front lip on the ⅞″ stock. ⅜″ wide gives the lip a 5/16″ overlap on the picture edge (⅜″ − 1/16″ clearance). That is enough to hide a ragged edge and hold the picture, and it leaves a ⅞″ wall behind it.

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Profile section

Parts and stick layout

The numbers

Derived Working Result

Shortcut for any picture: every piece is cut to the picture dimension + 1⅞″, measured long point to long point. 15⅝″ + 1⅞″ = 17½″; 11½″ + 1⅞″ = 13⅜″.

Cut list

Finished stock is ⅞″ × 1¼″, rabbeted before mitering. Lengths are long point to long point.

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Rails (top, bottom) 2 ⅞″ × 1¼″ × 17½″ 45° at both ends, long point on the outside edge
Stiles (sides) 2 ⅞″ × 1¼″ × 13⅜″ Same

Backing board 1 ⅛″ × 11½″ × 15⅝″ Hardboard, thin ply or foam-core
Retainers 6–8 Flexi-points or small turn buttons, about ⅛″ proud of the rabbet floor
Hanger 1 set Two D-rings (screws ≤ ½″ long, since the wall is ⅞″ thick) + picture wire, or one sawtooth hanger for a light frame

Stock to buy: the four pieces total 61¾″ of long-point length. Alternating the miters nests the pieces, so each shared cut saves 1¼″ and the stick only needs about 58½″ with kerfs (61¾″ − 3 × 1¼″ + 3 kerfs). Buy one 6′ length (5/4 stock milled to ⅞″ × 1¼″) so the corners share grain and about 13½″ is left for test cuts. Mill a little extra width for the rabbet setup pieces.

Build sequence

  1. Mill one straight stick to ⅞″ × 1¼″, longer than needed. Pick the best face as the front.
  2. Cut the rabbet first, on the whole stick: ⅜″ wide × ½″ deep on the back inside edge. Table-saw it in two passes, or use a router with a rabbeting bit. Test on an offcut: the leftover front lip should be ⅜″ thick.
  3. Ease the front edges with a light 1/16″ chamfer or sanding if you want. Do it now, while the stick is straight.
  4. Check the saw’s 45° with a square cut-off test: cut two scraps, join them, and measure against a 90° square. Fix it before cutting good stock.
  5. Cut the miters on a miter saw or sled with a stop block. Set the stop for 17½″ and cut both rails with the same setting, then reset to 13⅜″ for the stiles. Measure on the outside (long-point) edge, with the rabbet side up or down, but the same way each time.
  6. Dry-fit the four pieces. Check that the rabbet opening is 15¾″ × 11⅝″ and that its diagonals match at 19.58″. If they don’t, sneak up on the miters with a shooting board.
  7. Glue the miters. End grain drinks glue, so size each miter with a thin coat, wait a minute, then apply glue and clamp with a band or corner clamps. Check the diagonals again before it sets.
  8. Reinforce the corners, because a plain miter is a weak joint: ⅛″ splines (a contrasting wood looks good), loose tenons or at least a pair of 18-ga brads at each corner.
  9. Sand and finish before the glass goes in. Keep finish out of the rabbet where the glass sits.
  10. Assemble: glass, picture, backing, then the points or turn buttons. Fit the D-rings on the back of each stile about a third of the way down (the wall is ⅞″ thick, so use short screws) and run the wire.

8″ × 10″ 8⅛″ × 10⅛″ 7⅜″ × 9⅜″ 9⅞″ × 11⅞″ 11⅞″ / 9⅞″

Here rails are the long top and bottom pieces, and stiles are the shorter sides. With a mat, use the mat’s outside size as the “picture”.

For any other size, with or without a mat, use the picture-frame calculator: it gives the outside and inside length of every member, a cut list and a mat bill of materials, and prints to PDF.

Alternate rabbet

If a ⅜″-wide rabbet hides too much of the picture, a ¼″ rabbet is fine (the stock is the same size). Everything shifts by +¼″: sight opening 15¼″ × 11⅛″, outside 17¾″ × 13⅝″, so rails become 17¾″ and stiles 13⅝″ (formula: picture + 2⅛″). The lip then overlaps the picture by only 3/16″ per side.

Open questions

  • Rabbet size is my choice, not part of your profile. If the profile you have in mind already includes a rabbet or a decorative bevel on the front, tell me and I’ll redo the numbers.
  • Mat or no mat: if the picture is to be matted, the “picture” in every formula is the mat’s outside size, and the glass is cut to that.
  • Print thickness: a thick print or a stretched canvas needs a deeper rabbet. ½″ allows about 5/16″ of glass + print + backing.
  • Hanging weight: the D-ring setup suits anything up to the 5–10 lb range. A frame this size with glass weighs about 2–3 lb.

The look: square-section legs, a top that overhangs the ends by a lot and the front and back by a little, two wide drawers hung right under the top over a thin rail, end aprons with a shallow arch, and a lower shelf sitting on chunky end rails.

(est.) = measured off the maker’s photos or chosen by me, and the numbers to sanity-check before cutting. The top’s thickness is not known: I assumed 1″, so measure it first (see Open questions).

Tenon layout in the legs

At every leg two members come in from adjacent faces. Because each part sits flush to an outside face, the mortises are shallow in one direction and 1″ deep in the other, so they don’t cross. Staggering the heights anyway keeps the mortises well apart and leaves more wood in the leg, so no mitered tenon tips are needed. Measured down from the top of the leg:

Joint Tenon position Size

Build sequence

  1. Mill the legs from 8/4 and everything else to size. Let the stock sit between passes, since cherry moves.
  2. Cut the mortises and tenons using the table above. Keep the aprons flush to the leg outer faces.
  3. Cut the end-apron arch: a 1″ rise over 13½″ is an arc of radius about 23¼″. Bend a thin stick against two nails at the shoulders and a third at the 1″ rise to draw it, then bandsaw and fair with a plane or sanding block.
  4. Dry-fit the two end frames: leg pair + end apron + shelf end rail. Confirm the 13½″ shoulder distance and that the rail is flush to the leg outer faces.
  5. Glue up the ends, then join them with the back apron and the lower front rail. Dry-clamp first and check the 39″ opening and the 43″ × 17½″ frame for square.
  6. Fit the divider (into the rail) and the runner (divider to back apron). Check the two drawer openings are equal at 19⅛″.
  7. Screw on the slide spacers, glue on the shelf cleats and drop in the shelf. Screw the shelf to the cleats through slots so it can move across its 12¾″ width.
  8. Build and dovetail the drawers, fit the slides, then plane the fronts to a 1/16″ reveal all round.
  9. Turn and fit the knobs.
  10. Finish: scrape off all squeeze-out first, then hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax for cherry or walnut (tung oil and wax for maple), matching the maker.
  11. Attach the top with figure-8 fasteners or buttons so it can move seasonally; across its 19½″ width it will move roughly ⅛″–3/16″. Fix it at the middle of each end apron and let the other fasteners slide. Center it: 2½″ at each end, 1″ at the front and back.

Open questions

  • Top thickness: I assumed 1″. If yours differs, leg length is 18″ − thickness, and nothing else changes. A thicker top just looks heavier.
  • Top condition: is the top flat, and does it have breadboard ends or edge molding? Either would change the overhangs and how it is fastened.
  • Height: 18″ here; the maker’s is 22″. See The numbers for the 22″ changes.
  • Arch and shelf height: both estimated from photos. The arch is decorative only.
  • Frame joinery: the maker’s page doesn’t say how the legs and aprons are joined, so mortise-and-tenon here is my choice, to match the other plans on this site.
  • Space behind the drawers: about 2″ is left behind each box. Decide whether to leave it open or close it with a back panel.
  • Slides: pick them before cutting the runner and spacers. Some slides need more than ½″ per side.

item.title: Gravity Water-Filter Stand: Floor and Countertop (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build: a hardwood stand for a gravity-fed stainless water filter (Berkey, British Berkefeld or anything of that size). It comes in two heights from one construction: a floor stand with a shelf for a tumbler or pitcher under the spigot, and a countertop stand that lifts the filter just high enough to get a glass under it. Everything is square stock, mortise-and-tenon and table-saw cuts, with no turning, no compound angles and no curves.

The look comes from your two reference photos: four legs that rise past the platform as posts to keep the filter from walking off (the cherry stand), and a plain four-leg frame with the filter sitting down inside it (the ceramic-crock stand). The shelf for a tumbler is borrowed from the cherry one too.

Provenance of the numbers. (stated) = from you: a floor stand for a Berkey-sized filter, a countertop version too, built on a table saw. (maker) = the filter makers’ published sizes, rounded; sources disagree by up to an inch, so measure your own filter before cutting (see Fit). (chosen) = a design decision of mine. (derived) = worked out from those so everything closes. (est.) = a guess I couldn’t verify (spigot reach, weight), flagged in Open questions. The drawings come from tools/woodworking/water_filter_stand_drawings.py; change a constant there and the SVGs and cut-list numbers move together.

Renderings

Concept views drawn from the plan dimensions (a Big Berkey is shown). They are illustrations, not photographs. Click any figure to open it full size.

Floor stand

Countertop stand

Design in one paragraph

Four 1½″ square legs sit 14½″ apart outside (11½″ between). A ¾″ × 3″ apron is tenoned between them, with its top edge ¾″ proud of a drop-in plate, so the filter sits in a shallow tray whose walls are the aprons and whose four corners are the legs, which stand 3″ above the aprons as posts. Under the plate the aprons carry ¾″ cleats. A lower rail frame at the floor stand’s 6½–8½″ height supports a ¾″ shelf that reaches 9½″ to the front, so a tumbler can stand directly under the spigot. The countertop stand is the same top frame on 8″ legs with no front apron, so the cup can sit on the counter in front of the stand.

The feet taper on their two inside faces from 1½″ to 1″, which is the only shaped cut on the legs.

Fit: which filters this takes

The frame’s opening (between the aprons) is 12½″ square; the plate is 12⅜″. Filter sizes are the makers’ published figures, rounded (the Berkey site gives its own sizes, and retailers disagree by about an inch on height).

Filter Dia. Height Gap to apron, each side Total height, floor stand Total height, countertop

Big Berkey (2.25 gal) 8½″ 19¼″ 2″ 43¼″ 27¼″

Crown Berkey (6 gal) 11″ 30″ ¾″ 54″ 38″
  • Up to the Royal / British Berkefeld 12 L fits as drawn. Crown and Imperial are tight on width and very tall on the floor stand: widen the frame by 1″ (move the legs out ½″ each way: IN_HALF = 6.25) and, for the floor stand, drop the plate height to 20″ so the top lid stays under about 50″. The black base ring on a Berkey flares about ¼″ wider than the body, so check that too.
  • Why the 1″+ gap matters: the filter should drop in without scraping, and the base ring and spigot need room. The posts, not the gap, keep it from walking, so a loose fit is fine.

How the pieces close:

Derived Working Result

Both mortises in a leg are cut ⅝″ + 1/16″ deep into adjacent faces. The apron setback puts them 7/16″ from the outside arris, so the two cavities touch at one corner point but never overlap. All four legs are identical.

Cut list: floor stand

Stock: cherry, walnut, white oak or maple (the photos are cherry). Finished sizes; mill a little long and trim to length after the joinery is cut.

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 1½″ × 1½″ × 27¾″ Cut blanks 28¼″. Two mortises each (see the parts drawing); taper the inside faces below 6″; ease all arrises 3/16″

Plate 1 ¾″ × 12⅜″ × 12⅜″ Corners clipped 1⅛″ × 1⅛″ at 45°

Cut list: countertop stand

The same parts, with the front apron and lower rail frame left out and the legs and aprons shortened.

Part Qty T × W × L Notes

Aprons (left, right, back) 3 ¾″ × 2½″ × 12¾″ Tenon ⅜″ × 1½″ × ⅝″. No front apron
Plate 1 ¾″ × 12⅜″ × 12⅜″ Same shape as the floor stand’s. Plywood glued down braces the open front; see Plate below
Plate cleats 3 ¾″ × ¾″ × 10″ Under the plate on the left, right and back aprons. Cleat top at 7¼″
Feet 4 felt or rubber pads Protects the counter. A small dab of bumper adhesive is enough

Build sequence

  1. Mill the legs to 1½″ square (glue up 8/4 or laminate two 4/4 pieces if you only have thin stock; the grain shows on all four faces, so quartersawn or rift stock looks best). Mill the aprons, rails, plate, cleats and shelf stock to ¾″.
  2. Lay out all mortises on one leg and copy to the others. Both inside faces get one; they sit 7/16″ from the outside arris on each face. Use a story stick so the four legs come out identical. Cut the mortises ⅜″ wide × the heights in the cut list × 11/16″ deep (router and a fence, a hollow-chisel mortiser, or drill and chisel).
  3. Cut the tenons on the table saw. Make cheek cuts with a tenoning jig (the miter-slot tenoning jig on this site works) or a stack dado, then the shoulders on a crosscut sled with a stop block. Cut them ⅜″ thick, ⅝″ long. Fit to the mortise and ease the tenon’s edges so the apron seats fully.
  4. Taper the feet. Mark the line 6″ up the inside faces (5½″ for the counter stand) and the 1″ square at the foot. Use a table-saw taper jig for each inside face, or the band saw, and finish with a plane. Do this after the mortises, since the taper is below them.
  5. Cut the plate and shelf. Clip the plate’s corners 1⅛″ at 45° with the miter gauge. Cut the shelf to 14″ × 16½″, notch the four leg corners with a crosscut and a rip (or a jigsaw), and chamfer the front corners 1¼″. Notch 1/16″ oversize so it never binds on the legs.
  6. Glue the cleats to the apron inside faces, ¾″ × ¾″ × 10″, with their top edge 1½″ below the apron top (floor stand) or at 7¼″ (counter stand). Do this before assembly while the aprons are flat on the bench.
  7. Dry-fit, then assemble in two stages. Glue the two side frames first (two legs, top apron, lower rail each), check them square and identical, then join them with the front and back aprons and rails. Check the diagonals of the top frame between the apron inside faces: they should match at about 17⅝″ (12½″ × √2). Clamp across the legs. A drawbore pin (⅛″ dowel) in each tenon is cheap insurance for a stand that gets bumped.
  8. Fit the plate. Set it on the cleats and check the gap (1/16″ each side). Fasten it as described below. On the floor stand, fasten the shelf to the lower rails the same way.
  9. Sand and finish before the filter goes on (see Finish).
  10. Check for rock. Stand it on a flat floor or counter and shim or sand a foot if it rocks. Then wall-anchor it (see Stability).

Plate

The plate needs to stay put without trapping seasonal movement:

  • Plywood (¾″ hardwood-faced ply, edges banded or just oiled): glue and screw it to the cleats. It doesn’t move, and on the countertop stand it braces the open front.
  • Solid wood moves roughly ⅛″ across 12″ over a year. Screw it down with slotted holes in the cleats’ long direction, never glue it, and keep 1/16″ clear of the aprons. The countertop stand’s open front then relies on its glued and drawbored tenons alone. That is plenty for an 11″-tall stand, because there is little leverage to rack it, and a stretcher in the front would block the cup, so don’t add one.

Finish

Water will drip on this stand. Use something water-resistant: wipe-on or spray polyurethane, spar varnish, or a hardwax oil, with at least three coats on the plate, the shelf and the top edge of the aprons. Seal the underside of the plate and shelf as well as the top, or the unfinished side will cup. A stainless filter also sweats in a humid room; a thin cork or felt disk under the base ring keeps the finish from marking.

Stability and safety

  • Load: a full filter plus its water is roughly 30–65 lb depending on size (est.). The plate is ¾″ hardwood on cleats around all four edges; at that load it is plenty stiff. Don’t build it thinner.
  • Tipping: with a full Big Berkey on the plate (centre of mass about 32″ up), the floor stand tips at about 13° from vertical, so a hard shove at the top could do it. Anchor it to the wall: two small L-brackets (or a ⅛″ brass strap) from a back leg to the wall stud.
  • Countertop: it is low and stable on its own, but the total height is 27–34″, so check the clearance under any wall cabinet before choosing it. A Big Berkey is just over 27″ on it.
  • Posts: the 3″ posts are retainers, not a restraint. A child can pull a filter off by the spigot; if that matters in your house, anchor the stand and add a strap or a bracket.

Open questions

  • Spigot height and reach (est.): I used a spigot that sticks out about 2⅝″ and whose underside is about 2″ above the filter’s base. The front-apron top is ¾″ above the plate, which leaves about 1¼″ under the spigot. Measure yours with the filter in hand. If the spigot’s underside is less than about ½″ above the apron top, lower the front apron on the floor stand (make it 2″, or leave it out like the countertop stand).
  • Filter diameter and base ring: the table is the makers’ figures, rounded, and a base ring wider than the body can eat a ¼″ of the gap. Measure the widest point of your base.
  • Which filter and where it lives: the Imperial and Crown on the floor stand put the lid at 50–54″. If you refill from a standing position, drop the plate to 20″ (move the aprons, cleats and shelf with it), or choose a 6 gallon-class filter for the counter stand.
  • Tumbler under the spigot: the floor stand fits vessels up to 12½″ tall (to the underside of the front apron); the cup circle in the drawings is a 30 oz tumbler, 3¼″ across.
  • Shelf overhang: the shelf’s front tongue reaches 2½″ past the front rail so a cup can sit under the spigot. It is ¾″ hardwood, fine for a cup or a pitcher, but don’t load a gallon jug at the very edge.
  • Is the leg taper worth it? It is the only shaped cut. Skip it (straight 1½″ legs) and the stand is a little heavier-looking but no weaker.
  • Hardware: wall brackets, felt pads, plate screws and slotted-hole washers are not in the cut list.

item.title: Split-Top Roubo Bench + Table-Saw Outfeed (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build: a Benchcrafted-style split-top Roubo bench, 87″ × 24″ × 35″, with a Glide leg vise on a Crisscross Retro (owned) and a tail vise (to buy), set up so it also works as the outfeed table for a cabinet table saw. The saw is raised or lowered to meet the bench, so the bench height is chosen for hand work and the saw does the matching.

Starting point: the Benchcrafted Split-Top Roubo plan (archive), from its preview drawings. This page does not replace the plan: it keeps the plan’s envelope, adds what outfeed duty needs, and flags everything I could not read from a preview image.

Provenance of the numbers. (stated) = read off the Benchcrafted preview drawings or product pages. (chosen) = my design decision for outfeed use. (derived) = worked out so the stated ones close. (est.) = measured off a preview image or a single reseller figure; confirm against the plan and the hardware manuals before cutting. Drawings come from tools/woodworking/split_top_roubo_drawings.py; change a constant and re-run.

What changes for outfeed duty

  1. The saw end is plain. The bench’s left end faces the saw. It carries no vise, no end cap, no handwheel and no chamfer, so a long board slides off the saw table onto an uninterrupted surface. The tail vise goes at the far end, as in the Benchcrafted drawing, and the leg vise stays at the saw end of the front, so nothing sticks out where the work travels.
  2. The gap gets a bridge. The split-top’s 1⅝″ gap catches offcuts and the leading corners of panels. A loose 1-9/16″ × ¾″ bridge rests on two ⅜″ × ¾″ ledges and sits flush, so the whole top is one surface for sawing. Lift it out and the gap is back for clamps and the gap-stop.
  3. Dogs come out, holes stay low. The tail vise’s dog notches are ¾″ square in the front strip. Pull the dogs before ripping. The deadman and the front dog row are the only openings, and neither is on the centerline where the cut stock travels.
  4. It is never touched to the saw. Leave ¼″ of air at the saw end. Saw vibration should not couple into a 350 lb bench, and planing forces should not move the saw’s fence rails.
  5. Fine height trim. A ½″ leveling foot under each leg (±⅜″ of travel) gives a trim to the saw table, and takes up an uneven floor. Check flatness with a straightedge across both tables, saw blade lowered; aim for the top at or 1/64″ below the saw table, never above (a board edge should not catch).
  6. Finish. Oil and shellac only; no wax on the top. A waxed top is fast, but the wax gets onto every board and ruins glue-ups and finishes.

Match this to your saw: the drawings show a generic 27″-deep cabinet-saw table 35″ off the floor. Measure yours with a straightedge. A 24″ bench is narrower than your saw table, so line the bench’s centerline up with the blade, not with the table’s edge, for ripping. Panels wider than about 20″ still want a side support; this is a bench-height outfeed, not a sheet-goods table.

Drawings (true scale)

Front elevation, with the saw at the saw end

Plan

End elevation, from the saw end

Top cross-section: slabs, gap bridge, front build-up

Tail-vise layout

Dimensions

Tail vise

Hardware: the Benchcrafted Tail Vise (archive): an 18″ Acme screw, a 1″ sliding plate/nut, guide rails and a dog block. Facts from the maker’s pages: the vise was conceived for a top at least 4″ thick; the guide recommends a 3″ end cap; the tenon shoulder / cavity must be at least 13½″ so the screw can’t hit the end of its cavity; the sliding plate is reversible for a right- or left-hand bench. A reseller lists ~12¼″ of travel with a 2⅞″ cap and an 11¾″ capacity with a 5″ dog block; treat these as unconfirmed.

Layout used here:

  • Screw 5½″ from the front face (est.), running inside the front slab behind a dog strip with ¾″ square notches on a ~5″ pitch (est. from the preview), 14 notches from 12″ to 77″.
  • Front slab built back to front: main 7-3/16″, backing strip ¾″, dog strip 1½″, laminate 1¾″ (all est.). The notches are cut in the strip and closed by the backing.
  • End cap 3″ × 4″ × 24″, bolted through the slab ends with barrel nuts; the guide-rail mortises in it are cut after it is attached.
  • Handwheel on the far end only. At the saw end there is nothing.

The Benchcrafted plan has full dimensions for the end cap, rails and mortises, and the hardware ships with a template. Use those, not my layout lines, for the vise itself.

Leg vise

You already own the Glide on a Crisscross Retro (the version that uses brackets, so no deep top-pivot hole). Notes from the maker’s pages: the Crisscross takes 18″ of vertical space in the leg and chop; the Glide gives up to 9″ of jaw depth depending on the bench; keep the chop long at the top and trim it flush with the benchtop last. Mount it so the chop face stands proud of the benchtop’s front by the chop’s thickness, as in a classic Roubo.

Because the vise is at the saw end, the chop and handwheel are near where you stand when you rip. They are on the front face and below the top, so they don’t block the surface, but the screw end sticks out ~5″ and the open chop sticks out ~9″ more. Keep your feeding path clear of them, or move the vise to the other front leg (mirror the plan).

Materials and drying

Species. Soft maple for the top, legs, rails and chop. Southern yellow pine is the budget route, but only if it’s dry. Cherry is nice but expensive and gets dinged. Hard maple, beech or white oak go in the small wear parts. Weights are rough: ~350 lb in soft maple, ~290 lb in yellow pine.

Part Species Notes
Top slabs, legs, rails, ledgers, chop, deadman soft maple (or dense yellow pine) the bulk of the bench
End cap, dog strip, dog block hard maple, beech or white oak take the wear and the screw loads
Gap bridge and its ledges hard maple or oak stays flat; replaceable
Shelf boards pine or fir is fine not structural

Order ~140 bf of the main species and ~10 bf of the hard one, so there’s room to reject a bad board. Rail and ledger thicknesses are my estimates; check them against the plan’s cut list.

Buying.

  • 8/4 rough. Buy 6″-plus widths so you can rip them. Ask for #1 common or better with few knots.
  • Top. Rip 8/4 into 4¼″ strips and stand them on edge, about 7 strips per slab, edge-laminated. Alternate the growth rings to keep each slab flat.
  • Legs. Face-laminate two 8/4 boards to 3½″ thick.
  • Yellow pine. Ask for dense, tight-ringed, mostly heartwood stock. Big-box 2x lumber is typically only kiln-dried to about 19%, and it will twist as it dries.

Drying and moisture.

  • Target: 6–8% moisture, checked with a pin meter. Check several boards, not just one.
  • Acclimate: stack the stock flat with stickers in your shop for 3–4 weeks before milling.
  • Mill in stages: rough-mill, let it sit another week or two, then final-mill. Thick stock moves most right after it’s first cut.
  • Air-drying your own takes about a year per inch of thickness, so I’d buy dry stock for the top and only dry non-critical parts yourself.
  • After the build: the top will still move a little in its first season. That’s why the final flattening comes after the bench is assembled, then the saw is set to meet it.

Build outline

  1. Top slabs. Laminate or use solid slabs to 4″ thick; flatten before gluing the front strips. Dog strip first (the notches are cut on the bandsaw or table saw before gluing the backing on).
  2. Legs and rails. Drawbored mortise-and-tenons as in the Benchcrafted plan (3/8″ pins and barrel-nut bolts). Fit the leveling-foot inserts last.
  3. Vises. Fit the Crisscross and chop to the leg and the tail vise to the front slab before the top goes on the base.
  4. Ledges and bridge. Glue the ledges ¾″ below the top, 3/8″ wide; plane the bridge to fit with 1/32″ clearance each side and flush at the top.
  5. Flatten the top once everything is assembled, then set the saw to meet it.

Open questions

  • Your saw’s table height and rear edge. Does the rear of the saw have a rail or fence-rail tube that would clash with the bench end?
  • Which side does the saw’s fence stand? If you rip with the fence on the left, the cut stock leaves along the rear slab; check that the deadman and dogs are not in line.
  • Leg vise end. Saw end (as drawn) or tail end?
  • Plan details I couldn’t read: the chop thickness, tail-vise screw offset, guide-rail and end-cap mortises, and the dog pitch are est. Confirm against the plan and the hardware manuals (Crisscross Glide manual, 2025).
  • Sheet goods. The 24″ width won’t support a full sheet. A drop-down side extension is a possible later add.
